analysis.one_liner: Terminates the Seawolf nuclear attack submarine program, allowing only one sub already under contract.
analysis.headline: The bill to cancel the Seawolf submarine program died in the House Armed Services Committee without a vote, despite 7 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Representative Rick Santorum's bill would have directed the Defense Secretary to shut down the SSN-21 Seawolf attack submarine program, a Cold War-era nuclear submarine project. It would have allowed funding only for the single submarine already under contract, ending plans for more. It never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who would have been spared the cost of additional Seawolf submarines; at the time, the Soviet threat the sub was built to counter was ending.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Secretary of Defense to terminate the SSN-21 Seawolf attack submarine program outright [S2][S3].
Prohibits obligating funds to build any Seawolf beyond the single submarine for which a contract was already signed, stopping further production [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The shipyard and defense contractors building the submarines would lose work, and shipyard communities would bear the job losses; the Navy would forgo the additional boats.
analysis.who_pays_short: The submarine shipbuilder and its workers

drawbacks.text: Ending the program would have cost shipyard jobs and disrupted the industrial base for nuclear submarine construction, a cost an honest supporter had to acknowledge.
Critics of canceling new submarine production argued the Navy would still need modern attack submarines even as the Cold War ended, and a single-boat program raises per-unit costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have eliminated spending on additional Seawolf submarines just as the conflict they were designed for was winding down, saving public money at the cost of contractor work and some shipyard jobs. As a spending-cut measure, the balance tilts toward taxpayers, though the job losses were real.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to the House Armed Services Committee and its Seapower subcommittee, requested the Defense Department's comments, and then sat there until the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Representative Rick Santorum introduced the bill on March 26, 1992 [S5].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Armed Services [S5].
On March 31, 1992, the House requested an executive comment from the Department of Defense [S5].
It was referred to the Subcommittee on Seapower and Strategic and Critical Materials, where no further action was taken [S5].
Seven representatives cosponsored the bill, three Democrats and four Republicans [S4].
The bill received no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Seawolf program and its shipbuilder were better off: because the bill never moved, no production funding was cut and the status quo of ongoing construction spending continued.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The submarine program and its shipbuilder

for.name: Rep. Rick Santorum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to terminate the Seawolf program and sought support for it.

against.name: House Armed Services Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (Chair: Rep. Ronald Dellums)
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup or advanced the bill; it sat in committee and its Seapower subcommittee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Department of Defense
against.what_they_did: Was asked for its official comment on the bill; no endorsement followed.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan but small: 3 of the 7 cosponsors were Democrats and 4 were Republicans, and no floor vote ever occurred to reveal broader party positions.

industries.industry: Nuclear shipbuilding (Seawolf contractor, General Dynamics Electric Boat)
industries.note: The bill would have ended construction of additional Seawolf submarines, cutting off a major revenue stream for the contractor. The contractor's revenue came from taxpayer-funded defense contracts, so its interest in this bill ran against taxpayers' interest in lower spending.

Terminating a major weapons program would have signaled procurement cutbacks affecting the broader defense-contracting sector. Defense contractors' interest lies in keeping programs funded by taxpayers.
